country.name: Bolivia
country.tagline: Some of the world's highest vineyards, where wine and singani grow above 1,600 m on the edge of the tropics.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official national figure: 3,478 ha of grapes in 2024 (all uses). Tarija holds about 80 percent of Bolivia's wine industry; Correo del Sur (2021) put Tarija's grape area at about 5,000 ha. No reliable national wine-production figure; FAOSTAT carries only an outside estimate (about 8,000 t in 2023)

country.overview:
Bolivia makes wine in a place where vines should not grow: at 21°S, inside the tropics, but high in the Andes. Almost all vineyards sit between about 1,600 and 3,000 m, so the altitude replaces latitude, nights are cold and the sunlight is fierce. That combination gives aromatic grapes and deeply coloured reds, and it is the selling point of the small modern industry centred on the Tarija valley in the south of the country.

Vines arrived from Peru with Spanish settlers and missionaries in the 16th century to supply wine for Mass and for the booming silver city of Potosí. The earliest documented vineyards are in the Tarija valley around 1589 to 1590, and in the Cinti valley of Chuquisaca, where colonial haciendas trained vines up native molle and chañar trees, a practice that survives in vineyards 100 to 200 years old. For centuries most grapes went to *singani*, a fragrant brandy distilled from Muscat of Alexandria that Bolivia protects as a denomination of origin.

Modern winemaking dates from the 1960s and 1970s, when producers such as Kohlberg and Kuhlmann moved operations to Tarija and imported European technology. Today wineries including Kohlberg, Aranjuez, Campos de Solana, La Concepción, Casa Vieja and Magnus make Tannat, Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and aromatic whites, and a revival of old Criolla and Moscatel vines in Cinti has drawn attention abroad. Bolivia celebrates a national day of wine and singani on the last Friday of February.

history.title: First documented vineyards in Tarija
history.text: Documents of Luis de Fuentes y Vargas, founder of Tarija, mention vineyards in the Tarija valley, including at Tolomosa, the earliest records of vines in Bolivia.

history.title: Wine for Potosí
history.text: Vineyards in Cinti, Tarija and the valleys of Potosí department supply wine and aguardiente to the silver mines of Potosí, then one of the largest cities in the world.

history.title: First winery in Cinti
history.text: The first industrial winery is established at San Pedro near Camargo in Chuquisaca, starting with singani.

history.title: Tarija modernises
history.text: Producers such as Kuhlmann (which moves from Cinti to Tarija in 1973) and Kohlberg invest in European equipment; a national viticulture centre is created in 1986.

history.title: Singani denomination of origin
history.text: Law 1334 recognises Singani as a denomination of origin reserved for brandies made in defined valleys of Tarija, Chuquisaca, La Paz and Potosí.

history.title: National day of wine and singani
history.text: Bolivia establishes a national day of wine and singani, celebrated on the last Friday of February.

country.classification: Bolivia's only protected wine-sector name is the denomination of origin *Singani*, recognised by Law 1334 of 4 May 1992 and reserved for grape brandy distilled from Muscat of Alexandria wines produced, distilled and bottled in defined zones: the central valley and provinces of Tarija (Cercado, Avilés, Méndez, Arce), the Nor and Sud Cinti valleys of Chuquisaca, Luribay, Sapahaqui and the Loayza and Murillo provinces of La Paz, and valleys of Potosí department such as Cotagaita and Turuchipa. 'Gran singani' must come from grapes grown above 1,600 m. Wines carry place names (Tarija, Valle de Cinti) without a formal appellation system.
country.climate_soils: Bolivian vineyards are high-altitude, subtropical and semi-arid. In Tarija's central valley (about 1,700 to 2,100 m) days are warm, nights cool and rain falls mostly in summer; winds help dry the vines. Cinti, at about 2,400 m, is a narrow canyon of red rock. Intense ultraviolet radiation thickens grape skins and builds aromatics. Soils are alluvial and colluvial, derived from erosion of the surrounding peaks, with clay and sandy loams.

grapes.name: Muscat of Alexandria (Moscatel de Alejandría)
grapes.note: The main grape, used above all for singani.

grapes.name: Tannat
grapes.note: The leading quality red of Tarija, thick-skinned and suited to altitude.

grapes.name: Negra Criolla (Listán Prieto) and Vischoqueña
grapes.note: Colonial grapes surviving in old Cinti vineyards trained up trees.

grapes.name: Torrontés, Chardonnay, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.note: Aromatic and fresh whites at altitude.

further_reading: Wines of South America, Evan Goldstein

regions.name: Tarija
regions.summary: The Tarija valley produces about 80% of Bolivian wine and singani.
regions.history: Vineyards documented from 1589; modern wineries from the 1960s and 1970s.
regions.terroir: Semi-arid valley at 1,600 to 2,150 m; strong UV; summer rain.
regions.grapes: Tannat, Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Muscat of Alexandria.
regions.classification: Singani DO zone (provinces Cercado, Avilés, Méndez, Arce).

regions.history: Colonial haciendas; first winery at San Pedro in 1925; revival since 2000.
regions.classification: Singani DO zone (Nor and Sud Cinti).

bo-cotagaita-and-vitichi.name: Cotagaita and Vitichi
bo-cotagaita-and-vitichi.summary: Neighbouring valleys in Potosí department, with about 250 ha of vines (2008), roughly a tenth of Bolivia's vineyard, mostly traditional grapes for singani and local wine.

bo-samaipata.name: Samaipata
bo-samaipata.summary: Samaipata, in the Andean foothills of Santa Cruz department at about 1,700 m, is a young wine area near a famous pre-Inca site. Small wineries such as Uvairenda (Vinos 1750) and Landsuá make fresh reds and whites in a more humid climate.

bo-valle-central-de-tarija.name: Valle Central de Tarija
bo-valle-central-de-tarija.grapes: Tannat, Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Merlot, Moscatel de Alejandría, Torrontés
bo-valle-central-de-tarija.nerd_note: Tarija's Concepción valley in Uriondo is the hub of Bolivia's wine route, with adobe wineries and Casa Vieja's traditional cellar.
bo-valle-central-de-tarija.summary: The central valley of Tarija, at about 1,600 to 2,150 m, holds most of Bolivia's vineyards and wineries around the city of Tarija, Concepción (Uriondo), Santa Ana and La Pintada. A mild, semi-arid climate with summer rain, winds and cool nights favours Tannat, Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Muscat for singani. Kohlberg, Aranjuez, Campos de Solana, Casa Vieja, La Concepción and Magnus are based here.

bo-valle-de-cinti.name: Valle de Cinti
bo-valle-de-cinti.grapes: Negra Criolla, Moscatel de Alejandría, Vischoqueña
bo-valle-de-cinti.nerd_note: About 300 ha of vineyard in Cinti include around 30 vineyards with vines trained up living trees.
bo-valle-de-cinti.summary: The Cinti valley in Chuquisaca, around Camargo and Villa Abecia at about 2,400 m, is the spiritual home of Bolivian traditional winemaking. Its colonial vineyards, some 100 to 250 years old, climb native molle and chañar trees in a narrow red-rock canyon, a training system found almost nowhere else. Old Negra Criolla, Moscatel and Vischoqueña vines make singani and small-batch wines that have attracted a new generation of producers since 2000.

sites.name: Bodegas Kohlberg
sites.text: A family winery founded in Tarija by Julio Kohlberg, one of the pioneers of Bolivia's modern wine and singani industry. It is among the country's largest producers, with vineyards in the central valley.

sites.name: Bodegas Aranjuez
sites.text: A family winery on the outskirts of Tarija, Aranjuez is best known for Tannat grown at high altitude in the central valley. Its Tannat-based wines, notably the Juan Cruz label, helped bring Bolivian wine its first international recognition.

sites.name: Campos de Solana
sites.text: A Tarija winery on the road south to Padcaya, belonging to a family with a long singani tradition. Its wines include Tannat, Malbec and aromatic whites from vineyards in the central valley.

sites.name: Bodegas La Concepción, Uriondo
sites.text: A winery in the Concepción valley of Uriondo, south of Tarija, with vineyards at around 1,800 to 2,000 m, making high-altitude reds, whites and singani.

sites.name: La Casa Vieja, Concepción
sites.text: A traditional adobe winery in the village of Concepción, Uriondo, where wine is still made in old style and visitors eat under the vines; a centre of Tarija's wine route and harvest festivals.

sites.name: Villa Abecia, Cinti valley
sites.text: A village in the Cinti canyon of Chuquisaca where colonial-era vines climb native molle trees. Some vineyards here are over a century old, part of a landscape of adobe haciendas and singani stills.

sites.name: San Pedro, Camargo
sites.text: Site of Bolivia's first industrial winery, established in 1925 near Camargo in the Cinti valley by the Ortiz and Patiño families, which began with singani.
